Team 51, Area 51

A cow is fertile for only a few hours. Checks miss more than half. Cowllar watches the rest.

Know which animal needs attention — and when to inseminate. Cowllar monitors individual animals between staff observations and turns changes in their behaviour into a recommendation: an animal ID and an insemination window.

Miss one fertile period and
you lose 10,500 roubles and three weeks.

A cow will stand to be mounted for six and a half hours on average, and more than a third never do so at all. Miss that window and she waits about three weeks for the next one. Nobody can watch two hundred animals through a February night, so the calendar takes over and the guessing starts.

Move the sliders to your farm. Cows cycle roughly every 21 days, so each animal offers about 17 chances a year. Published miss rates in Russian herds run from 40 to 62 percent, and reach 83 percent in hard frost.

We asked four farms.
Three said yes.

Before any of this was built we sat with the people who would use it. These are their words, not ours. The one farm that said no has twelve cows and knows every one of them by name. Three of the four expressed interest in automated oestrus detection. Oestrus is the fertile period — the few hours a cow will stand to be mounted. That says the problem matters to them, and it is not a customer order.

We already have collars for activity and chewing, but they are inconvenient for the fertile period and we do not trust them. Pedometers were tried and they got lost. Skips happen often, and the cost is a longer service period, extra hormones and less milk. Health and fertility monitoring in one device would be ideal.

Seven interns told us the same story.

Students who spend their summers on farms, between them at ROTA AGRO, Sovkhoz im. Lenina, EkoNiva and RumelkoAgro. We asked what goes wrong with the method they use now.

Hidden oestrus, a considerable number of omissions.

Too many factors affect the behaviour and the reaction of the body. It is hard to keep track of the same cow, because they all move around the same shed, and for many of them the moment passes in a quiet phase. If a cow is sick or injured, attention goes there instead.

Inaccuracy.

What we promise the person
who walks the barn at 5 am.

Not a dashboard full of charts. Four plain commitments, each one testable on your farm.

01

We name the cow.

cow number, not a herd average

The alert says Cow 23, not "activity is elevated in group B". You walk to one animal, confirm, and inseminate.

02

We give you a window.

hours, not a herd average

The collar compares movement and rumination against that animal's own seven day baseline and, when it raises an oestrus alert, names the recommended insemination window — for example "Cow 23, today, 14:00 to 20:00". Those hours illustrate the interface, not a fixed recommendation for every animal. Opening the alert shows the changes that produced it.

03

It stays on your farm.

no internet connection needed

The collar transmits over the farm's own wifi to a server on site, and that server runs the behaviour and oestrus models and keeps the records. Internet access is unnecessary. Wifi coverage is required, and staff devices have to be able to reach the local server.

04

It listens as well as watches.

movement and sound together

Pedometers miss a quiet fertile period because it shows in few extra steps. Cowllar adds a microphone and analyses chewing and rumination alongside neck movement, which is where the quiet animals give themselves away. Whether sound catches oestrus that movement alone misses is the question our testing has to answer.

One person covers the whole herd.

On the farms we are aiming at, three hundred cows and up, a single veterinarian or reproduction technologist carries the breeding decisions. They do not need more numbers on a screen. They need to be told which animal to walk to, before the window shuts.

Everything on this page is built backwards from that one moment.

It keeps missing the quiet ones.

Six parts, one strap,
built by hand in Moscow.

Every component was chosen so the whole collar stays under fifty dollars in parts and keeps running with no network, no subscription and no cloud.

Motion, 25 times a second

A three axis accelerometer and magnetometer on the neck. Walking, standing, lying and mounting each leave a different signature. When a cow comes into her fertile period this signal doubles or triples, and that is the loudest thing on the animal.

From a shaking strap
to a name on your phone.

Four stages. The collar records and transmits over the farm's wifi; the behaviour and oestrus models run on a server on the farm. Tap a stage to see what happens to the signal.

Raw signal, 25 rows a second

The collar writes one row 25 times a second: three axes of acceleration, magnetometer, skin temperature and a sound level, each with a timestamp. A single day is about two million rows, which is why nothing useful happens until the next stage.

    We tested it on cows the model had never met.

    Six cows from a public Japanese dataset recorded at the same 25 Hz on the same part of the body. We trained on five and tested on the sixth, then rotated. No cow ever appears in both sides of the split, so nothing is memorised.

    79.1percent accuracy

    Pooled across all six held out cows, four behaviour classes, macro F1 of 0.67.

    best held out cow91.6%
    weakest cow56.8%
    What this proves today
    • The hardware records four sensors on a live animal for a full working day.
    • The pipeline runs end to end, from raw rows to a named behaviour.
    • Behaviour transfers across animals the model has never seen, at 79.1 percent.
    • The farmer can collect a day of data with a phone, standing next to the cow.
    What we have not earned yet
    • Oestrus alerts checked against a vet's confirmation. The scoring is wired, the labels are not collected.
    • Russian dairy breeds. Our validation cows are Japanese Black beef.
    • A week of continuous wear. Our record is eleven hours before the cow won.
    • More than one animal at a time. The July pilot is where that changes.

    Three days of one cow,
    in fifteen seconds.

    Press play. Movement climbs, chewing falls and the score crosses the line while there is still a day to act. What follows is demonstration data, labelled as such.

    Cow 23, hours 0 to 72

    Demonstration data. Modelled from published oestrus behaviour to show the scoring logic — the traces are an illustration, not a recording from an animal. A routine alert reads differently from a breeding recommendation: "Cow 23: movement and rumination below her usual levels. Check the animal." That names the change and claims no cause.

    Cow 23 is inside her normal range. The collar keeps counting and says nothing, which is most of the time and exactly the point.

    And this is the part the farmer actually opens.

    The dashboard reaches the farm server from the office or the barn. It opens with the herd overview: staff pick the animals carrying an oestrus alert or a movement and rumination alert, then open one profile. Each profile shows that animal's recorded behaviour over time against her own baseline, so a technologist can disagree with the machine before walking out to the barn.

    Eleven hours on a cow.
    Then she broke it.

    A partner farm in Moscow oblast let us strap an earlier prototype to an animal for a working day. We got the data out, and we got the failure we needed to design version two. What follows is earlier field experience: it informs the current work on attachment and recording quality, and it does not validate the design described on this page.

    What version two fixes,
    and who is doing it.

    The cow wrote our roadmap for us. Smaller, tougher, and worn by more than one animal for more than one day.

    Hardware

    • Smaller and lighter housing, less for a cow to catch and pull
    • Impact resistant shell instead of printed PETG
    • Strain relief on the temperature probe that fatigued
    • Battery gauge on board, so the farm sees charge before a deployment

    Data and model

    • A week long pilot on several cows in July
    • Vet confirmed fertile periods, the labels we are missing
    • Feeding class rebuilt, it is the weakest column in the matrix
    • Fine tuning on Russian dairy breeds, not only the public set

    On the farm

    • One base unit per barn, collars sync when the cow walks past
    • Phone alerts for the technologist who is already outside
    • Tie stall farms tested separately, where movement says less
    • Price held under fifty dollars of parts per collar
